Table of Contents. Why solid-state batteries matter, and why the timeline keeps slipping . First, what do we actually mean by “solid-state”? . Solid-state batteries for EVs timeline at a glance . 2024–2026: Lab breakthroughs, pilot lines, and first niche vehicles . 2027–2028: First solid-state EVs hit the road, barely . 2029–2030: The make-or-break bridge to real scale . 2031–2035: From flagship tech to a normal option box . How solid-state changes range, charging, and resale value . What this means if you’re buying an EV before 2030 . Checklist: Future-proofing your EV choice in a pre–solid-state world . FAQ: Solid-state batteries and EV buyers . If you believe the headlines, solid-state batteries for EVs are always “just three years away.” The truth is more complicated, and more useful, if you’re trying to decide whether to buy an electric car now, wait for the next generation, or hunt for a used EV that won’t be obsolete before the loan is paid off.. . The short version . Solid-state batteries are moving from lab benches to pilot production by the mid‑2020s, into a handful of expensive, low-volume EVs around 2027–2028, and toward meaningful mass-market adoption around 2030 and beyond . If you’re shopping for an EV in the 2026–2030 window, you are almost certainly buying a lithium‑ion car, with a long and useful life ahead of it.. . . . Why solid-state batteries matter, and why the timeline keeps slipping . Solid-state cells replace the flammable liquid electrolyte in today’s lithium‑ion batteries with a solid material. In theory, that unlocks three big advantages: higher energy density (more range for the same size pack), faster charging , and improved safety because you remove most of the liquid that can leak or ignite.. More energy in the same footprint could push mainstream EVs toward 500–700 miles of rated range, with halo products promising four figures. . Charging could move closer to the gas-station experience: 10–15 minutes to go from low state of charge back to a practical road-trip buffer. . Better thermal stability should reduce the risk of fires and potentially slow long-term degradation, which matters for resale value and second-life uses. . On paper, it’s the EV holy grail. In practice, solid-state has been delayed by exactly the things carmakers hate: fragile manufacturing yields, expensive materials, and the ugly realization that you can’t ship a cell that only works in a lab glove box. That’s why most serious players now talk about a phased rollout: pilot lines in the mid‑2020s, early commercialization around 2027–2028 , and mainstream mass production clustered around 2030+ rather than tomorrow morning.. First, what do we actually mean by “solid-state”? . Marketers toss around “solid-state” the way food brands use the word “natural.” To understand any timeline for solid-state batteries in EVs , you have to decode the labels.. Solid-state, semi-solid, and “solid-ish”: key definitions . Not every "solid" battery announcement means the same thing for real-world EVs. . . All-solid-state . Uses a fully solid electrolyte ; no liquid phase. This is what most engineers mean by "true" solid-state.. Promises the biggest gains in energy density and safety, but is also the most difficult to manufacture at scale.. . . . Hybrid / semi-solid . Mixes solid and liquid electrolyte phases. Sometimes branded as solid-state even though there’s still a small liquid fraction.. China’s 2026 national standard draws a hard line, limiting weight loss on heating to define what counts as fully solid.. . . . Advanced liquid lithium-ion . Improved cathodes, silicon-rich anodes, better separators, still liquid but with better performance.. Many 2025–2030 EVs will rely on this track while true solid-state matures in the background.. . . . . . Watch the fine print . Some automakers and suppliers quietly rebrand semi-solid or souped‑up liquid lithium‑ion cells as “solid-state.” When you see a press release, look for details about the electrolyte chemistry and whether the pack is actually in a customer car or just a demo cell.. . . . Solid-state batteries for EVs timeline at a glance . From lab to your driveway: key solid-state dates . . 2024–2026 . Pilot era . Automakers and startups run pilot lines and demo vehicles with solid-state or semi-solid packs. . . . 2027–2028 . First EVs . Highly priced, low-volume EVs debut with solid-state packs, mostly in Japan, China, and premium segments. . . . ~2030 . Mass production . Multiple analysts and battery executives cluster real mass-market ramp around 2030 and beyond. . . . 2031–2035 . Trickle-down . If timelines hold, solid-state options begin spreading into more affordable EV segments. . . . . Solid-state EV battery roadmap: 2024–2035 . A high-level view of how solid-state moves from pilot projects to real choices on a dealer lot. . Timeframe Stage What actually happens on the road . 2024–2026 Pilot & demo Pilot production lines, test fleets, some motorcycles and niche vehicles use solid or semi-solid cells. . 2027–2028 First commercialization Selective launch of EVs with solid-state packs, mainly higher-end or limited-run models. . 2029–2030 Early scaling More models in premium segments offer solid-state, but lithium-ion remains the dominant chemistry. . 2031–2035 Broader adoption Solid-state shows up as an option on more mainstream EVs; price and supply begin to normalize. . Post‑2035 Mature phase Assuming success, solid-state or its successors become just another line on the spec sheet. . . Dates are best-guess ranges based on current public plans and industry commentary, not guarantees. . . 2024–2026: Lab breakthroughs, pilot lines, and first niche vehicles . Right now, we’re in the messy adolescence of solid-state. The tech works in carefully controlled cells; the problem is making millions of them cheaply and reliably in real factories.. Automakers setting the stage. Toyota has government‑blessed plans in Japan to start limited solid-state production around 2026, with mass production targeted for "2030 and beyond." Early volumes will likely go into high-margin halo EVs rather than entry-level crossovers.. Nissan, Honda, Hyundai–Kia, VW Group/PowerCo are all running their own solid-state or semi-solid pilot lines with similar 2030-ish mass-market ambitions.. Chinese makers and cell suppliers are sprinting too, some already have semi-solid packs in demonstration vehicles and talk about installing all‑solid cells in the 2026–2027 window for specific high-end models.. . Suppliers and startups in the trenches. QuantumScape has shipped B‑sample solid-state lithium‑metal cells and signed a major industrialization deal with VW’s PowerCo, with a roadmap that steps through pilot production in the mid‑2020s toward commercial volume near the end of the decade.. Companies like Solid Power, SVOLT, Ganfeng, Ion Storage Systems and others are either building pilot lines or shipping early cells to aerospace, defense, and specialty customers.. China is preparing a national solid-state standard targeted for 2026, laying down definitions and test methods just as small-batch production ramps.. All of this is important groundwork, but very little of it translates into cars you can actually buy before 2027.. . . . How this affects a 2026–2027 EV shopper . If you plan to own your next EV for 5–8 years, you’ll likely trade it before solid-state becomes ubiquitous. Focus on a car with a proven lithium‑ion pack, good thermal management, and strong battery health, exactly what Recharged’s Score Report is built to highlight on every used EV we sell.. . . . . Solid-state batteries will arrive in stages: pilot lines first, then niche vehicles, and finally wider availability after 2030. 2027–2028: First solid-state EVs hit the road, barely . The late 2020s are when the PowerPoint decks finally meet pavement. Multiple automakers now point to 2027–2028 as their target for the first customer EVs with solid-state packs, usually in expensive, low-volume trims where buyers will tolerate risk and cost.. What 2027–2028 solid-state EVs will likely look like . Spoiler: they won’t be $32,000 compact crossovers at your local dealer, at least not yet. . . High-end, low-volume halos . Expect the first solid-state packs to show up in premium or performance EVs , think luxury sedans, performance crossovers, maybe limited-run sports cars.. These models soak up cost, generate PR, and give automakers real-world data without risking their bread-and-butter volume lines.. . . . Impressive specs, lots of asterisks . Headline numbers like "600+ miles of range" or "10‑minute fast charge" will be everywhere, but early packs may be power-limited, expensive, and supply‑constrained .. Don’t be surprised if most of these cars are sold out or allocated to specific markets while manufacturers quietly learn in the background.. . . . . . Industry insiders are cautious . At major battery conferences, Chinese cell makers and automakers have openly said that all-solid-state batteries won’t see true mass production before 2030 . Small demo fleets by 2027? Plausible. Every new crossover on your street riding on solid-state? Not this decade.. . . . 2029–2030: The make-or-break bridge to real scale . By 2029–2030, all the pilot lines and halo cars either add up to something real, or they get quietly folded into the museum of promising technologies that never quite scaled. Most serious forecasts cluster around this period as the first realistic window for meaningful, though still premium, mass production .. What needs to go right. Manufacturing yields must climb high enough that solid-state cells aren’t a financial sinkhole every time a defect appears.. Separator and electrolyte materials , often ceramic or sulfide-based, have to be made in bulk without eye-watering costs.. Automotive validation (crash, durability, abuse testing) has to be completed across multiple pack designs and vehicle platforms.. . What that means for car buyers. More EVs, especially in the luxury and near-luxury space, offer solid-state as an upgrade pack , similar to today’s "long-range" options.. Lithium‑ion sticks around as the workhorse chemistry , particularly for mainstream crossovers, trucks, and used vehicles.. Regulators and standards bodies finalize test methods and safety rules, making banks and insurers more comfortable with the tech.. . . 2031–2035: From flagship tech to a normal option box . If the cards fall the way automakers and cell suppliers hope, the early 2030s are when solid-state stops being a moonshot and starts being a line on a window sticker. That doesn’t mean every 2033 EV will use solid-state, any more than every 2026 phone uses the most exotic silicon. It means you’ll start seeing solid-state as a real choice in more than just flagship models.. Early-2030s outlook for everyday drivers . . More models . Segment spread . Compact SUVs, sedans, and maybe even some work trucks begin offering solid-state packs as range or towing upgrades. . . . Falling costs . Price pressure . Volume and manufacturing learning curves push solid-state closer to today’s lithium-ion pack prices. . . . New resale math . Used EV impact . Longer-lived packs and higher retained capacity start to reshape how the market values older EVs. . . . . By this point, the used EVs on sites like Recharged will include a mix of chemistries: proven lithium‑ion workhorses from the 2020s and early 2030s , alongside the first generation of solid-state cars coming off lease. Battery health diagnostics, already critical today, will become even more important in separating durable gems from early science projects.. How solid-state changes range, charging, and resale value . If the technology delivers as promised, solid-state will matter less because it’s “cool tech” and more because it quietly rewrites the ownership math: fewer compromises on range, shorter coffee breaks on road trips, and higher confidence that your battery won’t be a pumpkin at year ten.. Three big ownership changes solid-state could bring . Range, charging, and depreciation all get reshuffled. . . Range ceilings rise . With higher energy density, automakers can either increase range at similar pack sizes, or keep range steady and shrink/cheapen the pack.. Expect luxury and long-range trims to chase big numbers; mainstream models may just use the tech to save weight and cost.. . . . Charging compresses . Shorter charging times, especially in the crucial 10–80% band, make EVs more viable for road-trip diehards and commercial fleets.. Even if we don’t hit the most optimistic claims, shaving 30–40% off today’s DC fast-charge times is a tangible quality-of-life upgrade.. . . . Resale gets kinder . If solid-state proves more resistant to degradation, longer-lived packs could make 8–12‑year-old EVs much more attractive on the used market.. That also means tools that verify real battery health, like Recharged’s Score Report, become table stakes, not nice‑to‑have.. . . . . . Why used EV shoppers still win today . Even before solid-state, many modern lithium‑ion EVs lose surprisingly little capacity over their first 5–8 years when they’re well managed. What this means if you’re buying an EV before 2030 . All of this future tech is fascinating, but you still need to get to work on Monday. The risk many shoppers feel is, “If I buy a lithium‑ion EV now, will it be a flip phone the minute solid-state lands?” The answer, for most drivers, is no.. You’ll likely replace or trade your 2026–2029 EV before solid-state becomes the default chemistry across affordable segments. . Today’s lithium‑ion packs are already good enough for 200,000+ miles in many cases, especially in EVs with robust thermal management. . Charging infrastructure, connector standards (like NACS), and software will matter as much or more to day-to-day usability than the electrolyte inside the cells. . If you buy smart, choosing a model with a solid track record, verified battery health, and reasonable charging performance, you’re not buying a lame duck. You’re buying into a very active chapter of EV evolution, with a clear upgrade path when the next chemistry matures.. . The real mistake to avoid . The bigger risk isn’t “missing” solid-state. It’s overpaying today for a poorly documented battery. Whether you shop locally or online, insist on transparent battery health data before you sign. With Recharged, every used EV comes with an in‑depth Score Report, so you’re not guessing.. . . . Checklist: Future-proofing your EV choice in a pre–solid-state world . How to buy an EV today without losing sleep over tomorrow’s batteries . 1. Prioritize battery health over model year . A 3‑year‑old EV with a heavily abused pack is a worse buy than a 5‑year‑old car whose battery has been gently cycled and well cooled. Ask for state-of-health readings , DC fast charge history, and any warranty work. Recharged’s Score Report bundles this into one clear view. . . . 2. Look for strong thermal management . Liquid-cooled packs, smart preconditioning, and sensible charge curves are your friends. These design choices can matter as much as the chemistry when it comes to long-term degradation. . . . 3. Consider charging ecosystem, not just range . With NACS spreading and multi-network roaming improving, focus on how you’ll charge daily and on road trips. A car that plays nicely with major networks will age better than one with orphaned connectors or weak charging software. . . . 4. Think about your ownership horizon . If you tend to swap cars every 3–5 years, solid-state’s mass-market moment may still be in your next‑next vehicle. If you keep cars for a decade, buy something with a strong battery warranty and a pack that’s already known to age well. . . . 5. Don’t stretch for speculative tech promises . Be wary of paying a large premium today based on a brand’s vague promise to "upgrade" you to solid-state later. Until packs, standards, and warranties are nailed down, value what’s real: current performance, documented health, and total cost of ownership. . . . 6. Use experts who live and breathe EV data . If you don’t want to become a battery engineer in your spare time, lean on specialists. At Recharged, EV‑only advisors, battery diagnostics, and transparent pricing are baked into the process, so you can focus on the car, not the chemistry seminar. . . . . . Solid-state batteries are coming, but on the slow, industrial timescale of factories, standards committees, and cautious engineers, not the overnight pace of headlines. Through the 2020s, the smartest move isn’t to freeze and wait for perfection; it’s to buy well within the technologies that already work, using real data on battery health and total cost of ownership. Energy Green Energy . Climate . . Tesla Shop . Store . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Toggle dark mode . . . . . . CATL chief: solid-state batteries at ‘level 4 of 9,’ no leap until 2030. Fred Lambert | Jun 25 2026 - 8:27 am PT 69 Comments . . . . Robin Zeng Yuqun, the founder and chairman of CATL, the world’s largest EV battery maker, just poured cold water on the solid-state battery hype, saying the much-anticipated technology is only at “level four” of a nine-step readiness scale.. Speaking at “Summer Davos” in China this week, Zeng predicted that an inflection point for the technology won’t arrive until 2030 — and even warned that its commercial viability has yet to be established.. “Level four” out of nine. Zeng made the comments on Tuesday during a panel at the World Economic Forum’s Annual Meeting of the New Champions, held in Dalian, in northeast China’s Liaoning province. CATL confirmed his remarks on Thursday.. “Based on a measure of level one to nine, the technology has only reached level four so far,” Zeng said, according to a video clip posted online.. Advertisement - scroll for more content . He added that mass production of solid-state batteries — which use a solid electrolyte to conduct ions between electrodes instead of the liquid or gel found in conventional lithium-ion cells — would not begin until 2030.. “Even if the products are delivered, it remains to be seen whether they will be well received and become a commercial success on the market,” Zeng said.. Coming from the boss of the company that controls roughly 40% of the global EV battery market, that’s a notably cautious take on a technology that much of the industry has been hyping as the next great leap for electric vehicles.. But aren’t there already “solid-state” EVs on sale? Not quite. Here’s the nuance that gets lost in the hype: you can already buy EVs in China marketed with “solid-state” batteries — but they’re semi -solid-state, which is a fundamentally different thing from what Zeng is talking about.. Semi-solid cells still contain a liquid or gel electrolyte; they just reduce the amount. China’s draft national solid-state battery standard explicitly classifies semi-solid as a “mixed liquid-solid battery” — not a true solid-state battery. The all-solid-state cells Zeng pegs at “level four” remove the liquid entirely, which is exactly what makes them so hard to manufacture.. The semi-solid stuff is genuinely shipping. Nio began series production of 150 kWh semi-solid packs from partner WeLion back in April 2024 — though it reportedly pulled them after only a few hundred units on weak demand and high cost. IM Motors offers a 130 kWh semi-solid “Lightyear” pack in its L6 sedan, and SAIC’s MG4 became the first truly mass-produced semi-solid EV, hitting 100,000 units in eight months. Semi-solid packs now show up in sub-$15,000 electric SUVs in China .. So the technology that’s actually in customers’ driveways today is the watered-down version. The real leap in energy density and safety — all-solid-state — is the one Zeng says is still six years from mass production.. CATL’s own roadmap still points to 2027 — at small scale. Zeng’s skepticism isn’t a reversal so much as a reality check on timelines that have been creeping into marketing decks across the industry.. CATL is still working toward small-scale, all-solid-state production by 2027, with chief scientist Wu Kai previously outlining a goal of reaching “level seven to eight” by then and a planned capacity of just 5 GWh. The company has also already begun pilot production of solid-state cells with an energy density of 500 Wh/kg, roughly double that of today’s best liquid-electrolyte packs.. The gap between “small-batch” in 2027 and genuine “mass production” in 2030 is the whole point Zeng is making. He has said the odds of solid-state batteries reaching million-vehicle-level installations before 2030 are “very small,” and that getting there depends on three separate paths clearing at once: the technology, the product, and the commercial case.. We covered CATL’s ambitious solid-state patent filings earlier this year , and the company has been one of the most aggressive players in the space, teaming up with rival BYD to push the chemistry forward. But Zeng has consistently been more measured in public than the headlines his company generates.. Everyone else is saying 2027 — Zeng is saying watch the fine print. Zeng’s 2030 framing lands at a moment when nearly every major player is dangling 2027 as the breakthrough year.. Toyota, which holds more solid-state patents than anyone, has reiterated plans to launch EVs with all-solid-state batteries between 2027 and 2028, targeting driving ranges of around 1,200 km. BYD has confirmed it will begin putting all-solid-state batteries in vehicles in 2027 , with large-scale mass production slated for 2030. Volkswagen, Nio, and a wave of Chinese startups are clustered around the same window.. The catch is that “2027” almost always means a few hundred high-end vehicles, not a mainstream rollout. Toyota’s early output is expected to be measured in hundreds of tons of material — tens of thousands of vehicles at best, reserved for flagship Lexus models. China, meanwhile, keeps pushing the broader battery envelope on existing chemistry, from solid-state demonstrators hitting 1,000 km of range to CATL’s own LFP pack that recharges in six minutes .. Electrek’s Take. When the chairman of the world’s biggest battery company tells you the technology everyone’s betting on is at “level four of nine,” it’s worth listening — but it’s also worth knowing why he’s saying it.. Right now. Today. . . Solid state will be better, but perhaps just incrementally so. A little lighter, a little faster to charge, but not really revolutionary. Evolutionary.. . View all comments . Zeng has a long history of managing expectations in public while CATL spends billions racing toward the same finish line as everyone else. Some of that is genuine engineering humility: solid-state is brutally hard to manufacture at scale, dendrites and interface stability remain unsolved at volume, and “it works in a lab” is a very different thing from “it survives ten years and 200,000 km in a customer’s car.” On that, Zeng is simply right, and the industry’s 2027 hype deserves the cold water.. But there’s also a strategic angle. CATL has the most to lose if solid-state arrives early and resets the playing field, and the most to gain by keeping customers invested in its current LFP and sodium-ion roadmaps, which are real, shipping, and cheap. Talking down the timeline cools rivals’ marketing while CATL quietly builds its own 5 GWh line for 2027.. The honest read is somewhere in the middle: solid-state is coming, but it’ll trickle in through premium models first and won’t meaningfully move the EV market until the back half of this decade. Anyone promising a mass-market solid-state EV before 2030 is selling a roadmap, not a product. The Future of Solid-State Batteries: Are We Close to Mass Adoption?. By Manshi March 7, 2026 7 Mins Read . Facebook Twitter LinkedIn WhatsApp . . . . 🔊 Listen to Article . . Solid-state batteries are often described as the next generation of battery technology . Scientists, car manufacturers, and technology companies believe these batteries could solve many problems associated with current lithium-ion batteries . They promise longer driving range for electric vehicles , faster charging, improved safety, and longer battery life.. Because of these advantages, solid-state batteries are receiving enormous global investment from companies such as Toyota, BMW, Samsung, and many research institutions. However, while the technology is promising, many experts still question how soon these batteries will reach mass adoption.. This article discusses the most recent advancements, provides a straightforward explanation of solid-state battery technology, and assesses whether widespread adoption is actually imminent.. What Are Solid-State Batteries?. Lithium-ion batteries are currently used in the majority of electric cars and electronics. During charging and discharging, these batteries’ liquid electrolyte permits lithium ions to flow between the battery’s electrodes.. Solid-state batteries work in a similar way, but instead of using a liquid electrolyte, they use a solid electrolyte made from materials such as ceramics, polymers, or sulfides. This structural change improves performance and safety.. According to researchers, compared to liquid electrolytes used in traditional lithium-ion batteries , solid electrolytes are more thermally stable and non-flammable, greatly lowering the risk of battery fires.. Because of this design, solid-state batteries can also use lithium-metal anodes, which store more energy than the graphite anodes used in current batteries.. Why Solid-State Batteries Are Important. 1. Higher Energy Density . Higher energy density is one of solid-state batteries’ main benefits. The quantity of energy stored in a battery in relation to its weight is known as energy density.. Advanced solid-state batteries could reach around 450–500 watt-hours per kilogram (Wh/kg), significantly higher than many lithium-ion batteries used today.. Higher energy density means:. Longer driving range for electric vehicles. Smaller battery packs. Lighter devices and vehicles. Some prototype batteries already claim extremely long ranges.. As an illustration of the potential of next-generation battery technologies, a prototype semi-solid-state battery created by Chinese researchers reportedly achieved a driving range of over 620 miles (1,000 km) during testing.. 2. Faster Charging . Compared to modern lithium-ion batteries, solid-state batteries may charge considerably more quickly.. Some experiments show that electric cars with these batteries might be able to charge up to 80% in about ten minutes.. One of the main issues with the adoption of electric vehicles long charging times compared to petrol refueling may be resolved by fast charging.. 3. Improved Safety . Lithium-ion batteries contain liquid electrolytes that can catch fire if damaged or overheated.. Solid-state batteries reduce this risk because their electrolytes are solid and non-flammable, which improves overall safety.. This safety improvement is particularly important for:. Electric vehicles. Airplanes and aerospace systems. Consumer electronics. 4. Longer Lifespan . Solid-state batteries are also expected to last longer than lithium-ion batteries.. Studies indicate that advanced solid-state designs could attain more than 5,000 charge cycles, in contrast to approximately 1,000 to 2,000 cycles for numerous lithium-ion batteries.. A longer lifespan means:. Lower maintenance costs. Reduced battery replacement. More sustainable energy storage systems. The Global Race to Develop Solid-State Batteries. Many large companies and governments are investing billions of dollars to develop this technology.. Automotive Industry . Car manufacturers see solid-state batteries as a way to make electric vehicles more competitive with gasoline cars.. Several companies currently working on solid-state battery technology include:. Toyota. Nissan. BMW. Volkswagen. Hyundai. Ford. Toyota is one of the most active companies in this field. The company has been researching solid-state batteries since 2006 and holds more than 1,000 patents related to the technology.. Reports from the industry and the company say that Toyota plans to release electric cars with solid-state batteries around 2027–2028.. To support this goal, Japan’s energy company Idemitsu Kosan is building a lithium sulfide production plant, which will supply materials needed for solid electrolytes.. Battery Technology Companies. In addition to automakers, many specialized battery companies are also developing solid-state batteries.. These include:. QuantumScape. Solid Power. ProLogium. Samsung SDI. These companies focus on improving battery materials, manufacturing techniques, and performance.. Research Institutions . Researchers and universities all over the world are looking into solid-state batteries.. But scientists stress that there are still big technical problems that need to be solved before the technology can be used by a lot of people.. Major Challenges to Mass Adoption. Despite the promising benefits, several important challenges remain.. 1. Manufacturing Complexity . Producing solid-state batteries at large scale is extremely difficult.. The materials used for solid electrolytes must maintain excellent contact between battery components, which is harder than with liquid electrolytes.. Manufacturing processes must also be redesigned, which increases development time and costs.. 2. High Production Costs . Currently, solid-state batteries are much more expensive than conventional lithium-ion batteries.. Some estimates say that these batteries could cost almost three times as much as current battery technologies because they use complicated materials and manufacturing methods.. Reducing these costs is essential before the technology can reach mass markets.. 3. Technical Limitations . Researchers are still working to solve several technical issues, including:. Lithium dendrite formation (which can cause short circuits). Resistance between solid materials. Performance problems at different temperatures. Scientists say solving these issues is critical before large-scale commercialization becomes possible.. Timeline for Solid-State Battery Adoption. Although headlines often suggest that solid-state batteries are arriving soon, experts expect adoption to happen gradually.. Current projections suggest the following timeline:. 2025–2026 . Prototype vehicles and pilot manufacturing lines. Continued testing by automakers. 2027–2028 . First commercial electric vehicles with solid-state batteries. Limited production, mainly in premium vehicles. 2029–2030 . Larger production volumes. Potential cost reductions. After 2030 . Possible widespread adoption across the automotive industry. A look at the industry shows that widespread use could start by the end of the decade, when costs go down and production gets better.. Potential Impact on the Energy Industry. If solid-state batteries reach mass production, they could transform several industries.. Electric Vehicles . Solid-state batteries could remove three major barriers to EV adoption:. Limited driving range. Long charging times. Safety concerns. This would make electric vehicles more attractive to consumers.. Renewable Energy Storage . Renewable energy systems like solar and wind require efficient energy storage. Solid-state batteries could improve grid-scale storage systems, helping stabilize electricity supply.. Consumer Electronics . Smartphones, laptops, and wearable devices could benefit from:. Smaller batteries. Longer battery life. Improved safety. Solid-state batteries are one of the most exciting new technologies in the field of energy. They have a lot of benefits over regular lithium-ion batteries, such as more energy density, faster charging, better safety, and a longer lifespan.. Toyota and other big car companies are putting a lot of money into the technology, and new research breakthroughs show that it is making a lot of progress. Some car companies want to make the first cars with solid-state batteries in the next few years.. However, important challenges still remain, including high production costs, manufacturing difficulties, and unresolved technical issues.. So, while solid-state batteries are getting closer to being real, they probably won’t be widely used until the late 2020s or early 2030s.. In short, solid-state batteries are no longer just a fantasy, but they are still moving from the lab to real-world products. If researchers can get past the problems they are having now, these batteries could change the way electric cars, renewable energy storage, and consumer electronics work in the next few decades.. This could increase EV range by 50% for the same battery weight—a critical leap for mass-market adoption.. 350-500 Wh/kg — Projected energy density for solid state EV batteries, a 50-100% improvement over leading lithium-ion cells.. Solid state batteries can support ultra-fast charging, with some prototypes reaching 80% charge in under 15 minutes .. Safety is dramatically improved: the elimination of flammable liquid electrolytes reduces the risk of thermal runaway and catastrophic fires .. 3. Cost and Manufacturing Barriers. Current solid state prototype cells cost roughly 2-4x more per kWh than commercial lithium-ion packs due to materials and process complexity .. Scaling production from lab to gigafactory scale remains the primary bottleneck, as no company has yet demonstrated mass-market volumes at target cost.. 4. Industry Dynamics. Over 15 automakers and battery firms have announced solid state battery partnerships or pilot lines since 2023, but none have delivered a production EV powered by solid state cells as of early 2026 .. Early hype has driven significant capital inflows, but history shows that only a fraction of these entrants will survive the “valley of death” between prototype and profitable mass production.. Cycle Life (cycles) 1,000-2,000 2,500-5,000 . Safety (fire risk) Moderate Low . Cost ($/kWh) $100-120 $200-400 . . *All figures for solid state are based on prototype or pilot line data, not commercial-scale production. *. Case Study: Toyota’s Solid State Battery Pilot, Japan 2025. In August 2025, Toyota Motor Corporation unveiled its first solid state battery pilot line at its Motomachi plant in Toyota City, Japan. The pilot facility, a joint venture with Panasonic, was designed to validate solid state battery production at a pre-commercial scale. The company announced that the cells achieved energy densities of 450 Wh/kg and could be charged to 80% in 12 minutes. However, executives acknowledged that manufacturing yields remained below 60%, and the cost per kWh exceeded $300—triple that of Toyota’s mainstream lithium-ion packs. The pilot line produced several hundred prototype packs, which were installed in concept vehicles for durability testing. Despite the technical milestone, Toyota stated that solid state batteries would not appear in commercial EVs before late 2027, citing unresolved production and cost barriers .. Analytical Framework: The S3 Model — “Scale, Stability, Standardization”. To systematically evaluate the trajectory of solid state battery adoption in EVs, this article introduces the S3 Model:. Scale : The ability to move from pilot lines to mass production, with yields above 90% and costs below $150/kWh.. Stability : Ensuring cell durability, cycle life, and safety are proven in real-world automotive environments (5+ years, 2,000+ cycles).. Standardization : Establishing interoperable formats, supply chain agreements, and regulatory certification for widespread industry adoption.. An EV battery innovation only triggers a true “revolution” once all three pillars are in place. The S3 Model predicts that most current solid state initiatives are stuck between “Stability” and “Scale”—with “Standardization” lagging, as no industry-wide format yet exists.. Predictions and Outlook. PREDICTION [1/3] : The first commercially available solid state battery electric vehicle from a major automaker will not reach mass-market consumers before Q4 2028. (70% confidence, timeframe: by December 2028). PREDICTION [2/3] : By 2030, fewer than 20% of new EVs sold globally will feature solid state batteries, with the remainder still relying on advanced lithium-ion chemistries. (65% confidence, timeframe: by December 2030). PREDICTION [3/3] : Two-thirds of early solid state battery startups active in 2025 will either exit the market or be acquired by larger battery or automotive firms by 2031, as consolidation accelerates. (70% confidence, timeframe: by December 2031). What to Watch. Announcements of gigafactory-scale solid state lines with confirmed cost and yield data, not just lab or pilot milestones.. Regulatory moves on battery safety, recycling, and supply chain transparency, which could accelerate or slow adoption.. Shifts in Asian, European, and US industrial policy—especially subsidies or tariffs—that favor local battery manufacturing.. The first solid state-powered EV recalls or safety incidents, which could shape public and market perceptions.. Historical Analog. This evolution closely mirrors the lithium-ion battery adoption in the 1990s-2000s: both technologies entered with immense hype, faced major engineering and cost barriers, and only achieved mass-market success after a decade of scaling, shakeout, and standardization. Many early lithium-ion players failed or were absorbed, with the ultimate winners being those that mastered manufacturing and supply chain integration—not just those who led in basic research.. Counter-Thesis. The strongest argument against a gradual, multi-year adoption curve is the possibility of a sudden inflection point—triggered by a major breakthrough in solid electrolyte chemistry or automated manufacturing—that collapses cost curves and enables exponential solid state EV adoption within just 2-3 years. Proponents argue that advances in AI-driven materials discovery or massive state-backed investment (particularly in China) could compress timelines. However, the persistent gap between lab-scale performance and gigafactory-scale yields—demonstrated repeatedly in battery history—suggests that these technological surges rarely bypass the hard realities of scaling and process engineering.. Stakeholder Implications. Regulators/Policymakers. Action : Prioritize funding and incentives for domestic gigafactory construction, not just R&D, to ensure national competitiveness in battery manufacturing.. Action : Update battery safety, transport, and recycling standards to accommodate new solid state chemistries and formats.. Action : Monitor and address potential supply chain concentration risks, especially around critical raw materials for solid electrolytes.. Investors/Capital Allocators. Action : Focus capital on firms with credible scale-up plans, proven pilot yields, and established partnerships with major automakers, rather than speculative early-stage startups.. Action : Diversify across the battery supply chain—including materials, recycling, and manufacturing automation—to hedge against technology risk.. Action : Prepare for a phase of consolidation and M&A; early hype cycles are likely to be followed by shakeouts.. Operators/Industry (Automakers, Battery Firms). Action : Invest in flexible manufacturing infrastructure that can support both advanced lithium-ion and solid state cell formats to maintain supply chain resilience.. Action : Pursue joint ventures and licensing agreements to share risk and accelerate technical learning.. Action : Begin pilot deployments in limited fleets (e.g., luxury or commercial vehicles) to gather real-world data on durability and safety before full-scale rollouts.. Frequently Asked Questions. Q: What is a solid state battery and how does it differ from lithium-ion? A: A solid state battery uses a solid electrolyte instead of the liquid or gel found in conventional lithium-ion batteries. This design can deliver higher energy density, faster charging, and greater safety because it eliminates flammable components and allows for thinner, more compact cells.. Q: When will solid state batteries be available in mass-market electric vehicles? A: Based on industry announcements and current progress, mass-market EVs with solid state batteries are unlikely before late 2028. Early models may appear in premium or limited-run vehicles sooner, but full market penetration will be gradual as manufacturing and cost challenges are addressed.. Q: Are solid state batteries safer than current EV batteries? A: Yes, solid state batteries are inherently safer because they eliminate the liquid electrolyte, which is flammable and can lead to thermal runaway fires in lithium-ion batteries. However, real-world safety data at scale is still limited, as no large fleets have yet been deployed.. Q: Will solid state batteries make EVs much cheaper? A: In the near term, no—solid state cells currently cost significantly more than lithium-ion packs due to manufacturing complexity. Over time, as production scales and processes mature, costs are expected to fall, but this transition will take several years.. Q: Which companies are leading in solid state battery development? A: Major automakers like Toyota, Volkswagen, and Ford, alongside battery specialists and startups, have active solid state programs. However, no company has yet achieved mass-market, cost-competitive production as of 2026.. Synthesis. Solid state battery technology is poised to transform the electric vehicle landscape, but the revolution will be evolutionary, not instantaneous. Breakthroughs in energy density, charging speed, and safety are real—but must be matched by manufacturing scale, cost reduction, and industry standardization. The next five years will separate hype from reality, as only a handful of players will emerge from the coming shakeout to define the new battery order. The future of solid-state batteries in electric vehicles: from innovation to commercial reality . Solid-state batteries (SSBs) promise significant advances in electric vehicle technology but their commercial success hinges primarily on achieving competitive pricing rather than just performance improvements. This report emphasizes the critical role of cost in the transition from laboratory innovation to market adoption. . . . July 23, 2026 . By Fastmarkets Metals , Connor Watts , and Luke Sweeney . . Automotive Battery materials Electric vehicles Policy and regulations . . . Fastmarkets contributed to the latest Next10 Insights SSB Technology Insight , bringing an independent price and market perspective to one of the most closely watched developments in battery technology in electric vehicles. . This contribution was led by Fastmarkets analysts Connor Watts , battery raw material demand analyst, and Dr Luke Sweeney , senior analyst, battery raw materials, whose insights help anchor the report’s technology discussion in market reality. . The report brings together cross-industry expertise to assess the future of solid-state batteries (SSBs). But one theme sits at the center of the analysis, and it is where Fastmarkets’ contribution is most critical: . The transition to solid-state will not be determined by performance alone. It will be determined by price. . The Future of Solid-State Batteries in Electric Vehicles: Read the report here. . Solid-state batteries: technology promise to price reality . Solid-state batteries have moved beyond laboratory validation and into pilot-scale development, with OEM roadmaps pointing toward initial commercialization later this decade. . Yet the gap between technical feasibility and commercial viability remains substantial. Fastmarkets’ analysis anchors this gap in a simple but powerful framework: . Conventional lithium-ion, particularly LFP, already sets a low-cost benchmark. In China, LFP cells were priced at $54.63 per kWh in April 2026, a figure that has climbed 13.6% year on year, reflecting upstream pressure rather than cost maturity stalling. . In Western markets, the premium is pronounced: cross-location modeling from Fastmarkets’ Battery Cost Index shows that the same LFP cell produced in Germany, the US, Poland or Hungary carries a substantially higher cost structure than its Chinese equivalent, with materials assumed to be shipped from China in all cases. . Solid-state must not just compete technologically. It must close this cost gap at scale. . This defines the competitive reality. SSBs are not entering a vacuum. They are entering a market already shaped by chemistries with established, if increasingly pressured, cost structures. . The Fastmarkets threshold: key EV market signal for scale . Within this context, Fastmarkets introduces a key market signal: a provisional threshold of $85 per kWh as a proof-of-concept benchmark for mass-market scalability. . This is not an arbitrary figure. It serves three critical analytical functions. . First, it provides a tangible point at which solid-state production can begin to demonstrate industrial credibility, even before achieving full parity with lithium-ion. . Second, it allows stakeholders to track progress from pilot production to early commercial runs to scalable manufacturing using a consistent cost benchmark. . Third, it reframes the debate away from open-ended technological timelines and toward observable economic milestones. The $85 per kWh figure is not the destination, but it is a necessary checkpoint on the path to commercial adoption. . To understand how demanding that checkpoint is, current lithium-ion data provides useful grounding. Among NCM chemistries in China, NCM-811, the lowest-cost ternary option, was priced at $66.89 per kWh in April 2026, up 14.8% year on year. NCM-622 reached $72.21 per kWh. . Solid-state cells must therefore achieve costs within roughly 25–30% of today’s lowest-cost incumbent before reaching the $85 threshold, and must do so with far less mature supply chains and manufacturing infrastructure. . Why cost and not performance will be the gating factor . The Next10 analysis highlights a structural tension across expert views. Some participants frame scaling as an execution challenge, solvable through yield improvements, process innovation, and supply chain maturation. Others emphasise the steep cost curve required to compete with incumbent chemistries. . Fastmarkets’ contribution bridges these perspectives. The core insight is that cost and manufacturability are inseparable. Low yields produce higher unit costs. Immature supply chains produce pricing volatility. Material constraints, in solid electrolytes and separator materials, produce cost inflation. . The BCI’s cost structure data for conventional lithium-ion illustrates what a mature version of this problem looks like. For an NCM-811 cell made in China in April 2026, cathode active material (CAM) alone accounted for 58.7% of total cell cost. . Within that, lithium represented 17.6% of total cost and nickel 17.4%. These input dependencies are not managed through engineering alone. They are managed through scale, contracted supply, and sustained market transparency, all of which take years to develop. . Solid-state faces the same structural challenge, amplified by the immaturity of its own input markets. . Pricing signals across the SSB value chain . The report makes clear that pricing pressure is not confined to the cell level. It will emerge across the full SSB value chain. For materials, critical inputs, particularly solid electrolytes and separator materials, remain immature markets with limited scale. . The BCI data for conventional cells shows that even established separator and electrolyte markets for lithium-ion contribute a combined 6.7% to NCM-811 cell costs. For SSBs, analogous inputs will carry significantly higher unit costs until volume develops. . For manufacturing, production yields remain insufficient for cost-efficient large-scale output. The BCI’s manufacturing cost model, which covers 45 manufacturing inputs including CAPEX, equipment, labor and energy, shows that for NCM-811 cells in China, operational costs account for 10.5% of the total cell cost even at gigafactory scale. For SSB producers still in pilot phase, these proportions will be materially higher. . For architecture, innovations such as anodeless designs may reduce manufacturing complexity and improve cost structures over time. . Together, these factors reinforce a central conclusion. Cost competitiveness will only emerge through coordinated progress across materials, process, and scale, not through a single breakthrough. . The geopolitical layer . A further dimension that the BCI data makes concrete: cost trajectories for any battery chemistry are not solely a function of technology maturity. They are exposed to geopolitical supply disruption. . The May 2026 BCI documents several active pressures on conventional lithium-ion costs. The conflict in the Strait of Hormuz has disrupted aluminium metal supply, pushing up current collector costs.. With roughly 9% of global aluminium supply originating from Gulf states, smelting capacity has been directly affected in some cases by Iranian drone strikes. US-Iran tensions have simultaneously disrupted sulfur supply, which underpins the cost of sulfuric acid, a key reagent in phosphorus refining. . Fastmarkets estimates that 51% of China’s sulfur supply is sourced from countries whose refining capacity was affected by the conflict. . DRC export constraints continue to support cobalt prices despite broadly rangebound trading, while China’s dominance in graphite production keeps natural graphite markets structurally stagnant even as synthetic graphite costs rise on stronger ESS demand. . These are not marginal dynamics. They are structural features of the critical minerals landscape that any next-generation battery technology, including solid-state, will inherit and must price into long-term cost modeling. . Tracking the price tipping point . Fastmarkets’ pricing framework aligns with several observable market signals identified in the report: cell costs approaching or falling below approximately $85 per kWh, convergence on a dominant electrolyte or separator system, demonstration of high manufacturing yields, and validation of cost parity with high-nickel lithium-ion cells. . The BCI’s forward-looking cost forecasts offer a reference point for the last of these. For Q2 2026, Fastmarkets forecasts base case NCM prismatic production costs of $63.9 per kWh and LFP prismatic costs of $54.6 per kWh, both higher than the previous quarter’s forecast of $61.0 and $51.0 per kWh, respectively. . Upward revisions were driven by lithium price increases , higher nickel and cobalt sulfate costs for NCM cells, and other materials costs. Manufacturing costs saw a modest reduction of approximately $0.3 per kWh for both chemistries as automation investment is modeled to continue. . These signals matter because they are measurable, comparable and market-facing. . A more realistic timeline for solid-state battery adoption . The report suggests a phased pathway: demonstration and pilot deployment from 2026 to 2028, niche commercialization from 2028 to 2030, and potential broader adoption in the early 2030s, contingent on cost and scale milestones. . From a pricing perspective, this timeline reinforces a critical point. Adoption will accelerate not when the technology is proven, but when it is priced competitively. . The BCI’s long-range forecast to 2031 shows base case lithium-ion costs continuing to evolve, with other materials costs, lithium and manufacturing automation all playing roles in the trajectory. Solid-state must demonstrate a plausible path to cost parity with a target that is itself moving. . Fastmarkets’ role: bringing price transparency to emerging markets . As a knowledge partner, Fastmarkets’ contribution to this report reflects a broader role in the energy transition: defining price benchmarks for emerging technologies, tracking cost curves across evolving supply chains, and providing independent signals to guide procurement, investment, and strategy. . In a market where narratives often focus on performance breakthroughs, Fastmarkets adds a necessary counterbalance, a clear, data-driven view of when technologies become commercially viable and under what conditions. . Market decision on battery technology . Solid-state batteries represent a genuine step change in battery technology, with clear potential advantages in safety, energy density, and design flexibility. But as this analysis makes clear, their future will not be decided in the lab. . It will be decided in the market, at the point where cost, scale, and supply chain maturity align. That moment will be visible first, not in technology announcements, but in price signals.. Liam Critchley , Contributing Writer September 10, 2026. . . schedule 18 Min Read . . . LiCAP Technologies' solid-state battery manufacturing process. Image: LiCAP Technologies. . . . . The solid-state vs lithium-ion battery debate—or solid-state vs lithium-ion, depending on your preference—has been ongoing for many years. For many, solid-state batteries represent the future of the EV industry because of their better safety and higher energy density compared to most Li-ion batteries. Lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) batteries have changed the landscape in recent years as they offer much higher safety than nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) batteries. However, while the energy density of LFP continues to increase, it still falls behind NMC, and solid-state batteries are seen as the way to combine both energy density and safety (and faster charging) into a complete package. . Despite the promises of solid-state technology, the mass commercialisation of all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) has not yet happened. Small-scale production is expected in the back end of the 2020s with true full-scale mass manufacturing occurring from 2030 onwards. A number of automakers are already making the move, as are multiple dedicated battery manufacturers. . Related: From hours charging to ‘barely a couple of minutes’: Yuma Energy on the benefits of battery swapping . As it stands, several 'solid-state' batteries have been making it to market already, however, these are not true ASSBs and are instead semi-solid-state batteries—also known as quasi-solid state or hybrid solid state batteries. There's nothing wrong with semi-solid-state batteries and they represent an important part of the transition towards ASSBs, but the two should not be conflated together as their properties do differ. The true ASSBs will be making it into automakers' EVs in the coming 5-10 years. . Lithium-ion vs solid-state batteries: What's the difference?. The chemistry of a solid-state battery is fundamentally different to that of a Li-ion battery. While the named main difference between a lithium-ion vs solid-state battery is the electrolyte, the whole cell makeup is actually completely different. . Electrolyte composition . The electrolyte changes from an organic liquid electrolyte of lithium salts in Li-ion batteries to a solid material. Where a liquid electrolyte in Li-ion batteries is often a lithium salt, such as LiPF₆, LiBF₄, LiTFSI, LiFSI, or even an ether or carbonate-based liquid, the solid electrolyte in solid-state batteries is often made of a ceramic material, including oxide and sulphide ceramics, but also polymers and inorganic salts. A solid electrolyte is more stable and safer (as there is no chance of leakage), whereas a liquid electrolyte has this risk and needs to form a solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer on the anode (which, while beneficial, can lead to uncontrolled 'dead lithium' growth). . Related: EV battery fire risk: The complete statistical analysis . Separator material . One of the other main differences is the separator material. In Li-ion chemistries, a polymer separator is used, whereas a solid-state battery doesn't have a traditional separator material. Because there is no liquid to keep separate inside the cell, the solid-state electrolyte dual functions as a separator. . Electrode chemistry . Because the electrolyte and separator are different to conventional Li-ion batteries, it enables different electrode chemistries to be exploited. The cathode is similar with lithium-based oxides and phosphate materials dominating, but solid-state electrodes can use higher voltage cathode materials because solid-state batteries have better stability at higher voltages. The anode is where the biggest difference is for lithium-ion vs solid-state battery electrode chemistry. . Li-ion batteries have long used graphite as it is very stable and electrochemically efficient. However, the higher stability of solid-state batteries means that they can accommodate anodes that are lot more energy dense, including lithium metal anodes and graphite-silicon composite anodes, that allows more energy to be stored in the same volume of electrode material. . Related: LFP vs NMC battery technology: A buyer's guide for EV fleet infrastructure . Because non-conventional electrode materials can be used, it opens solid-state batteries to a wider range of cell design choices. So, while the costs are much higher now because the manufacturing scale is not on the same level as Li-ion manufacturing, the long-term could see solid-state batteries becoming cheaper once robust supply chains are in place—especially as the potential for different electrode materials means that some of the geopolitical tensions and supply chain risks can be mitigated a lot easier than Li-ion batteries. . Performance comparison: Key metrics. The following table compares the key performance metrics for lithium-ion vs solid-state batteries. These are generic ranges, as the actual values can vary based on the size of the battery, the specific battery chemistry, and the manufacturing process/who the manufacturer is. . . Energy density and range: Solid-state vs lithium-ion. The gravimetric energy density of the average Li-ion battery is 150–300Wh/kg whereas the anticipated target solid-state battery energy density is set at 400–500+ Wh/kg, with some reports saying that the energy density could reach up to 800Wh/kg. In terms of volumetric energy density, the solid-state battery energy density is anticipated to be 700–900Wh/L compared to a Li-ion energy density of 400–750Wh/L. . Li-ion batteries do have an upper theoretical energy density limit of 400–500Wh/kg, so they could theoretically be compatible with the average solid-state battery, but safety and cycle life issues make reaching these levels difficult. The other point to note is that these are cell-level energy densities, and the actual energy densities at the EV pack level tend to be around 30–40% lower than the cell energy density. This is because the packaging, cooling, wiring, and casing reduce the effective pack energy density because they add weight to a given volume without adding energy density. . The other factor when comparing solid-state battery energy density against Li-ion energy density is that there are many commercial Li-ion battery chemistries, all with a different energy density range. So, while the average for Li-ion batteries overall is 150–300Wh/kg and 400–750Wh/L, this can be further broken down into averages for each Li-ion cell chemistry: . LFP: 90–160Wh/kg and 200–350Wh/L . . . . NMC: 150–250Wh/kg and 400–600Wh/L . . . . NCA: 200–260Wh/kg and 500–700Wh/L . . . . . Why solid-state has higher energy density. The solid-state battery energy density is higher than Li-ion because lithium metal anodes have a higher energy density than conventional graphite anodes. This is because lithium metal anodes can store more energy per unit of volume/mass with a gravimetric specific capacity of 3,862 mAh g⁻¹, a volumetric specific capacity of 2,093 mAh cm⁻³ and a low reduction potential of −3.05 V versus a standard hydrogen electrode. All these properties directly contribute to a higher cell voltage and a higher energy density. . In addition to this, the solid electrolyte enables higher voltage cathode materials to be used without risking dendrite formation. This means that the cells can be made thinner and more compact so more energy can be stored in the same volume/weight. Using the high voltage cathodes and high-capacity anodes means that solid-state battery energy density could be 30–80% higher than Li-ion batteries. . Range implications . This higher energy density leads to a longer driving range for EVs and/or lighter EV battery packs. The solid electrolyte structure enables better ion flow between the electrodes, leading to higher efficiency and therefore higher energy density and range as the range is directly related to how much energy the battery can hold—and the more it can hold, the more it can discharge, leading to energy being released over longer time periods and driving distances. In terms of the average solid-state vs lithium-ion range, it's expected that the average solid-state range will be 500–750 miles compared to 250–350 miles without increasing battery weight or size. . Is solid-state safer than lithium-ion?. Outside the energy range, one of the defining performance metrics of solid-state batteries is their safety because there is no flammable liquid electrolyte. EV battery fires, while rarer than internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicle fires, are notoriously difficult to extinguish. The commercial development of LFP batteries has significantly improved the safety characteristics of Li-ion batteries because they can withstand higher temperatures and are a lot more resistant to mechanical abuse. However, they still contain liquid electrolytes, so solid-state batteries are still seen as the next frontier of battery safety. . Material phase advantages . Solid-state battery safety lies in the material phase of the electrolyte. Liquid electrolytes used in Li-ion batteries are very flammable, so short-circuiting and thermal runaway can quickly descend into fires and explosions. Liquid electrolytes are also highly susceptible to undergoing side reactions at the electrolyte-electrode interface, resulting in the formation of dendrites that quickly degrade battery performance and make short-circuiting more likely. Higher energy density Li-ion cells, such as NMC, are much more likely to undergo thermal runaway and catch fire compared to LFP. . Solid-state batteries are a lot more stable, have a high resistance to dendrite formation and are less likely to catch fire or undergo thermal runaway because the solid material is much more resistant to higher temperatures than liquid electrolytes. Having no liquid electrolyte and replacing it with a solid material directly reduces the flammability risk of the battery. This also means that electrolyte can't leak out of the cells, further reducing the potential fire risk when a battery becomes punctured or damaged—which is why solid-state batteries don't undergo thermal runaway during the nail penetration test unlike the majority of Li-ion cells. The solid electrolyte also has a high melting point so is unlikely to burn unlike liquid electrolyte which catches fire very easily. . Temperature tolerance . Aside from the electrolyte itself, removing the separator also helps to reduce the chance of the battery catching fire. Separators are sensitive to high temperatures but removing them means that solid-state batteries can operate in a wider temperature range without safety issues arising. This not only allows solid-state batteries to operate safely at internal temperatures up to 80°C compared to Li-ion—which struggle to remain safe above an internal temperature of 50°C—but the thermal safety of solid-state batteries mean that they will be able to charge at faster rates as the extra generated heat during fast charging won't have as many adverse effects compared to Li-ion batteries. . Dendrite suppression . However, the safety characteristics are not just limited to solid-state vs lithium-ion thermal characteristics. Dendrite formation is also a critical part of the safety discussion. In Li-ion batteries, lithium ions from the electrolyte deposit unevenly on the surface of the anode, and once a nucleation site has been established, side reactions continue to add more lithium, leading to the formation of needle-like lithium chains called dendrites throughout the liquid electrolyte. The dendrites eventually grow enough that they pierce the separator membrane, connect the electrodes, and short circuit the cell causing thermal runaway. . While dendrite growth is still possible in solid-state batteries, their growth is significantly suppressed because of the mechanical properties of the cell. The rigid solid electrolyte has a high mechanical strength and therefore a high mechanical resistance to dendrite formation. The ceramic and sulphide compounds in the electrolyte are too hard for dendrites to penetrate, physically blocking dendrites from penetrating through the electrolyte and short-circuiting the cell. This leads to uniform lithium deposition on the electrode-electrolyte interface, and the only way that dendrites can penetrate through a solid-state electrolyte is if there are voids or grain boundaries for the dendrites to grow into and exploit. . Charging speed and lifespan compared. Charging speeds are continuing to improve for Li-ion batteries, especially with the likes of BYD now bringing flash charging to everyday EVs, enabling charging in under 10 minutes. This is currently the gold standard of Li-ion fast charging, and the average is much lower. As it stands, solid-state batteries are still firmly in development and have not been optimised to the level that Li-ion batteries have, so both semi-solid-state and solid-state battery charging speeds are currently below that of Li-ion batteries. . Future charging potential . However, with solid-state batteries containing both lithium metal anodes and high voltage cathodes, there is the potential for solid-state batteries to charge faster than Li-ion batteries in the future due to having a higher ionic conductivity—as this will help to facilitate faster energy charging rates. On the other hand, companies are currently marketing semi-solid-state batteries as 'solid-state', but while they have a higher energy density and safety, their charging rates might not be any better than Li-ion because of their mixed electrolyte structure which could limit ion migration. When ASSBs emerge commercially, it is likely to be a different story as they will just have a solid network to promote ionic conductivity. . As noted above, the average Li-ion EV fast charges from 10–80% SOC in 22–35 minutes, whereas it's anticipated that the average 10–80% SOC solid-state battery charging speed will be 10–15 minutes. . Cycle life advantages . When it comes to cycle life, solid-state battery cycle life is set to outperform Li-ion cycle life. While some cells like LFP have been designed for longevity and have a much higher cycle life, the average solid-state battery is going to last a lot longer than the average Li-ion battery with slower degradation rates. The average Li-ion battery lasts for 1,000–2,000 cycles before noticeable capacity loss, while solid-state battery cycle life could exceed 3,000–5,000 cycles before significant capacity loss occurs due to lower internal chemical reactivity and stress. For semi-solid-state batteries, the cycle life sits in between the two, with 1,500–2,500 cycles before noticeable capacity loss. . It should be noted that while these values for charging speeds and cycle life for ASSBs have been claimed by some manufacturers, because they are not yet at a stage of mass commercialisation, these claims cannot yet be independently verified at scale. . When will solid-state batteries actually be available?. As it stands in 2026, any 'solid-state' battery currently available today is semi-solid-state hybrid design and not a true ASSB. While it's great talking about the potential benefit of using solid-state batteries for EVs, one of the biggest questions is, when will solid-state batteries be available? The solid-state battery commercialisation timeline looks set to rapidly increase in the coming years, with the late 2020s (mostly around 2027–28) seeing many automakers and battery manufacturers undergoing small-scale production, while 2030 onwards will see these companies enter full-scale manufacturing. . A lot of progress has been made by automakers and battery manufacturers towards the commercialisation of solid-state batteries, and their commercial reality is now just around the corner. The progression will naturally start with lower volumes of vehicles, with luxury models in traditional automakers and luxury brands likely to be first to equip them due to the initial added cost before large-scale manufacturing is established. Once the scale is established, then the costs will come down and we will see mass production of the batteries and solid-state EVs. This will be at least by 2030, but could be as late as 2035 for some automakers, as different companies are working to different solid-state battery commercialisation timelines based on their current state of internal development. . Japanese automakers leading the charge. There's a lot of activity in Japan from the major legacy automakers. Toyota has stated that it aims to have its first solid-state batteries manufactured somewhere between 2027 and 2028, with them being included in its first vehicles by 2028. Toyota has claimed that its new solid-state battery will provide a 20% increase in range over the Toyota Performance battery and is expected to deliver 1,000 km of driving range and a 10–80% charging time of 10 minutes, with a second generation planned for further down the line with 1,200 km driving range. . . Honda has stated that it plans to integrate solid-state batteries within the second half of 2020s, whereas Nissan already has an operational pilot plant line, with plans to launch solid-state battery EVs with an 800Wh/L volumetric energy density by 2028. On the other hand, Hyundai Motor Group is working towards longer solid-state battery commercialisation timelines, with no plans to launch solid-state battery EVs before 2030. . Chinese manufacturers accelerating development. As expected, there is also a lot of activity over in China, where the majority of EV batteries are already manufactured and where new battery innovations tend to first be commercialised at scale. Geely, a Volvo subsidiary, has plans to have a solid-state battery pack completed by 2026 with a 400Wh/kg energy density. On the other hand, Dongfeng has already completed a 0.2GWh production line, with batteries ready for vehicle use from this year onwards. Dongfeng has set mass-production targets for 2027 with the expectation that its first battery pack will deliver 350Wh/kg energy density and 1,000 km range. Developments are already taking place to develop a new battery pack with a 500Wh/kg energy density. . GAC Motors, one of the leading companies developing commercial-level graphene-based EV batteries, has plans to integrate solid-state batteries into its EVs sometime this year, with mass production planned for 2027–2030. It's expected that the batteries will provide between 500–1,000+ km depending on the EV. Qingtao Energy is planning to deliver solid-state batteries at scale by 2027, with energy densities of at least 400Wh/kg. . BYD has been doing some serious innovation with its Blade Batteries, and the Blade Battery 2.0 has become one of the highest performance Li-ion systems today. Nevertheless, BYD are still innovating in the solid-state battery space and plans to have its first EVs integrated with solid-state batteries in 2027. There are plans to follow this up with a demonstration phase between 2027–2029 and mass production targets have been set for 2030. . Global automakers joining the race. There are also many other global automakers with solid-state batteries on their commercialisation radar in the next 5–10 years. Mercedes Benz has started testing solid-state batteries developed in partnership with Factorial Energy. It's expected that the batteries will provide a driving range of at least 620 miles, and both mass production and market introduction targets have been set for before 2030. . BMW has been testing solid-state cells in its BMW i7 range and has since formed a partnership with Samsung SDI to support commercialisation. As it stands, BMW is planning to have solid-state batteries mass-produced by 2030. Karma Automotive is planning to launch one of the first 'ultra-luxury super cars' with a solid-state battery by 2027. Karma Automotive has stated that the first vehicle to use its solid-state battery will be the Karma Kaveya super-coupe. This is a big transition and statement as Karma Automotive doesn't currently manufacture battery EVs but does offer PHEVs. . Independent battery manufacturers. Outside of automakers who have dedicated their R&D teams to developing new solid-state batteries, there are also many independent battery manufacturing companies that are set to supply automakers with solid-state batteries as well. . Back in China, the largest battery manufacturer in the world, CATL, currently has a conservative solid-state battery commercialisation timeline with small batch production by 2027 and mass production by 2030. . In South Korea, SK On opened a pilot plant back in 2025 and is planning for mass production and commercialisation of 800Wh/L solid-state batteries by 2029. Between 2026 and 2028, SK On is going to be focused on pilot-scale development and OEM integration ahead of large-scale manufacturing. As noted above, Samsung SDI are working with BMW but are also targeting 900Wh/L anode-free solid-state battery mass production by 2027 after success with the pilot line in Suwon. It's expected that the batteries will first be used in premium vehicles in 2027, and while there are claims of mass production, it's expected that the volumes in 2027 will still be small. Samsung SDI already supplies semi-solid-state batteries. . Finally, QuantumScape, who are backed by Volkswagen, is planning small-scale production in 2026 with mass production in 2027–2028. QuantumScape claims that its anode-free solid-state batteries have an 844Wh/L volumetric energy density, 301Wh/kg gravimetric energy and a 10–80% charge time of around 12 minutes. The company has claimed that EVs that achieve 350 miles on current Li-ion batteries could achieve up to 500 miles of range using its solid-state cells. . Frequently Asked Questions. Is solid-state safer than lithium-ion? . Yes. Solid-state batteries use a solid electrolyte instead of a flammable liquid one, which removes the main driver of thermal runaway and fire risk. They are also far more resistant to dendrite formation and can operate safely at higher internal temperatures (up to 80°C versus roughly 50°C for Li-ion), making them the next major step up in EV battery safety. . When will solid-state batteries actually be available? . Small-scale production is expected in the late 2020s, mostly around 2027-2028, from automakers including Toyota, Nissan, and BYD. True full-scale mass manufacturing of all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) isn’t expected until 2030 onwards, with some automakers not reaching mass production until 2035. Batteries marketed as “solid-state” today are typically semi-solid-state hybrids, not true ASSBs. . What solid-state batteries mean for EV charging infrastructure. So, with solid-state batteries on the horizon in the next 5–10 years, what does this mean for charging infrastructure? . There will need to be some EV infrastructure planning for solid-state batteries, but there won't necessarily need to be any dedicated solid-state battery charging infrastructure in the near-term. EVs with solid-state batteries will still be able to use the same charging standards (CCS, NACS, J1772), meaning that infrastructure compatibility is not going to be an issue. . Grid management considerations . While the charging speeds are not as high as Li-ion yet, in the future, they could become greater. At this point, charging station owners might have to think about their infrastructure as faster charging speeds could affect station throughput planning and dwell-time assumptions, as well as draw shorter but larger loads from the grid—which will need to be planned for and managed as this could lead to higher power spikes that could put pressure on the grid if a lot of these spikes happen all at once or for long time periods. For infrastructure owners, the safer batteries will mean that there is less fire risk, so multiple ultra-fast chargers on a site will eventually pose less of a fire risk as the ratio of EVs with solid-state batteries on the road increases. . Station design evolution . With different types of batteries on the road, charging stations will need to be able to accommodate EVs with differing voltages and power requirements so that power can be delivered safely and reliably. It will also mark a shift in consumer behaviour because there will be fewer stops for EV drivers. This could mean that charging stations might need to be redesigned to accommodate the shorter dwell times, because while drivers might stop less, the faster charging times could lead to a higher throughput of vehicles each day—so the layout should be maximised to make it easy for EVs to go in and out quickly. The increase in throughput could lead to higher returns for charging station owners and less downtime for fleets. . Energy storage integration . However, because of the potential for the high throughput to cause a lot of power spikes, either at once or continuously throughout the day, on-site renewables and BESS will have to become standard to act as a buffer to these spikes and prevent the destabilisation of the local grid. Some charging stations are already equipped with renewables and BESS but their integration as key energy assets is only going to increase as more solid-state battery EVs hit the road. . . .
