Solid-state vs lithium-ion batteries: EV timeline compared . With major automakers targeting 2027-2030 for commercialisation, EV infrastructure planners need to understand the realistic timeline and implications of solid-state batteries for charging networks.. . . . . Liam Critchley , Contributing Writer September 10, 2026. . . schedule 18 Min Read . . . LiCAP Technologies' solid-state battery manufacturing process. Image: LiCAP Technologies. . . . . The solid-state vs lithium-ion battery debate—or solid-state vs lithium-ion, depending on your preference—has been ongoing for many years. For many, solid-state batteries represent the future of the EV industry because of their better safety and higher energy density compared to most Li-ion batteries. Lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) batteries have changed the landscape in recent years as they offer much higher safety than nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) batteries. However, while the energy density of LFP continues to increase, it still falls behind NMC, and solid-state batteries are seen as the way to combine both energy density and safety (and faster charging) into a complete package. . Despite the promises of solid-state technology, the mass commercialisation of all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) has not yet happened. Small-scale production is expected in the back end of the 2020s with true full-scale mass manufacturing occurring from 2030 onwards. A number of automakers are already making the move, as are multiple dedicated battery manufacturers. . Related: From hours charging to ‘barely a couple of minutes’: Yuma Energy on the benefits of battery swapping . As it stands, several 'solid-state' batteries have been making it to market already, however, these are not true ASSBs and are instead semi-solid-state batteries—also known as quasi-solid state or hybrid solid state batteries. There's nothing wrong with semi-solid-state batteries and they represent an important part of the transition towards ASSBs, but the two should not be conflated together as their properties do differ. The true ASSBs will be making it into automakers' EVs in the coming 5-10 years. . Lithium-ion vs solid-state batteries: What's the difference?. The chemistry of a solid-state battery is fundamentally different to that of a Li-ion battery. While the named main difference between a lithium-ion vs solid-state battery is the electrolyte, the whole cell makeup is actually completely different. . Electrolyte composition . The electrolyte changes from an organic liquid electrolyte of lithium salts in Li-ion batteries to a solid material. Where a liquid electrolyte in Li-ion batteries is often a lithium salt, such as LiPF₆, LiBF₄, LiTFSI, LiFSI, or even an ether or carbonate-based liquid, the solid electrolyte in solid-state batteries is often made of a ceramic material, including oxide and sulphide ceramics, but also polymers and inorganic salts. A solid electrolyte is more stable and safer (as there is no chance of leakage), whereas a liquid electrolyte has this risk and needs to form a solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer on the anode (which, while beneficial, can lead to uncontrolled 'dead lithium' growth). . Related: EV battery fire risk: The complete statistical analysis . Separator material . One of the other main differences is the separator material. In Li-ion chemistries, a polymer separator is used, whereas a solid-state battery doesn't have a traditional separator material. Because there is no liquid to keep separate inside the cell, the solid-state electrolyte dual functions as a separator. . Electrode chemistry . Because the electrolyte and separator are different to conventional Li-ion batteries, it enables different electrode chemistries to be exploited. The cathode is similar with lithium-based oxides and phosphate materials dominating, but solid-state electrodes can use higher voltage cathode materials because solid-state batteries have better stability at higher voltages. The anode is where the biggest difference is for lithium-ion vs solid-state battery electrode chemistry. . Li-ion batteries have long used graphite as it is very stable and electrochemically efficient. However, the higher stability of solid-state batteries means that they can accommodate anodes that are lot more energy dense, including lithium metal anodes and graphite-silicon composite anodes, that allows more energy to be stored in the same volume of electrode material. . Related: LFP vs NMC battery technology: A buyer's guide for EV fleet infrastructure . Because non-conventional electrode materials can be used, it opens solid-state batteries to a wider range of cell design choices. So, while the costs are much higher now because the manufacturing scale is not on the same level as Li-ion manufacturing, the long-term could see solid-state batteries becoming cheaper once robust supply chains are in place—especially as the potential for different electrode materials means that some of the geopolitical tensions and supply chain risks can be mitigated a lot easier than Li-ion batteries. . Performance comparison: Key metrics. The following table compares the key performance metrics for lithium-ion vs solid-state batteries. These are generic ranges, as the actual values can vary based on the size of the battery, the specific battery chemistry, and the manufacturing process/who the manufacturer is. . . Energy density and range: Solid-state vs lithium-ion. The gravimetric energy density of the average Li-ion battery is 150–300Wh/kg whereas the anticipated target solid-state battery energy density is set at 400–500+ Wh/kg, with some reports saying that the energy density could reach up to 800Wh/kg. In terms of volumetric energy density, the solid-state battery energy density is anticipated to be 700–900Wh/L compared to a Li-ion energy density of 400–750Wh/L. . Li-ion batteries do have an upper theoretical energy density limit of 400–500Wh/kg, so they could theoretically be compatible with the average solid-state battery, but safety and cycle life issues make reaching these levels difficult. The other point to note is that these are cell-level energy densities, and the actual energy densities at the EV pack level tend to be around 30–40% lower than the cell energy density. This is because the packaging, cooling, wiring, and casing reduce the effective pack energy density because they add weight to a given volume without adding energy density. . The other factor when comparing solid-state battery energy density against Li-ion energy density is that there are many commercial Li-ion battery chemistries, all with a different energy density range. So, while the average for Li-ion batteries overall is 150–300Wh/kg and 400–750Wh/L, this can be further broken down into averages for each Li-ion cell chemistry: . LFP: 90–160Wh/kg and 200–350Wh/L . . . . NMC: 150–250Wh/kg and 400–600Wh/L . . . . NCA: 200–260Wh/kg and 500–700Wh/L . . . . . Why solid-state has higher energy density. The solid-state battery energy density is higher than Li-ion because lithium metal anodes have a higher energy density than conventional graphite anodes. This is because lithium metal anodes can store more energy per unit of volume/mass with a gravimetric specific capacity of 3,862 mAh g⁻¹, a volumetric specific capacity of 2,093 mAh cm⁻³ and a low reduction potential of −3.05 V versus a standard hydrogen electrode. All these properties directly contribute to a higher cell voltage and a higher energy density. . In addition to this, the solid electrolyte enables higher voltage cathode materials to be used without risking dendrite formation. This means that the cells can be made thinner and more compact so more energy can be stored in the same volume/weight. Using the high voltage cathodes and high-capacity anodes means that solid-state battery energy density could be 30–80% higher than Li-ion batteries. . Range implications . This higher energy density leads to a longer driving range for EVs and/or lighter EV battery packs. The solid electrolyte structure enables better ion flow between the electrodes, leading to higher efficiency and therefore higher energy density and range as the range is directly related to how much energy the battery can hold—and the more it can hold, the more it can discharge, leading to energy being released over longer time periods and driving distances. In terms of the average solid-state vs lithium-ion range, it's expected that the average solid-state range will be 500–750 miles compared to 250–350 miles without increasing battery weight or size. . Is solid-state safer than lithium-ion?. Outside the energy range, one of the defining performance metrics of solid-state batteries is their safety because there is no flammable liquid electrolyte. EV battery fires, while rarer than internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicle fires, are notoriously difficult to extinguish. The commercial development of LFP batteries has significantly improved the safety characteristics of Li-ion batteries because they can withstand higher temperatures and are a lot more resistant to mechanical abuse. However, they still contain liquid electrolytes, so solid-state batteries are still seen as the next frontier of battery safety. . Material phase advantages . Solid-state battery safety lies in the material phase of the electrolyte. Liquid electrolytes used in Li-ion batteries are very flammable, so short-circuiting and thermal runaway can quickly descend into fires and explosions. Liquid electrolytes are also highly susceptible to undergoing side reactions at the electrolyte-electrode interface, resulting in the formation of dendrites that quickly degrade battery performance and make short-circuiting more likely. Higher energy density Li-ion cells, such as NMC, are much more likely to undergo thermal runaway and catch fire compared to LFP. . Solid-state batteries are a lot more stable, have a high resistance to dendrite formation and are less likely to catch fire or undergo thermal runaway because the solid material is much more resistant to higher temperatures than liquid electrolytes. Having no liquid electrolyte and replacing it with a solid material directly reduces the flammability risk of the battery. This also means that electrolyte can't leak out of the cells, further reducing the potential fire risk when a battery becomes punctured or damaged—which is why solid-state batteries don't undergo thermal runaway during the nail penetration test unlike the majority of Li-ion cells. The solid electrolyte also has a high melting point so is unlikely to burn unlike liquid electrolyte which catches fire very easily. . Temperature tolerance . Aside from the electrolyte itself, removing the separator also helps to reduce the chance of the battery catching fire. Separators are sensitive to high temperatures but removing them means that solid-state batteries can operate in a wider temperature range without safety issues arising. This not only allows solid-state batteries to operate safely at internal temperatures up to 80°C compared to Li-ion—which struggle to remain safe above an internal temperature of 50°C—but the thermal safety of solid-state batteries mean that they will be able to charge at faster rates as the extra generated heat during fast charging won't have as many adverse effects compared to Li-ion batteries. . Dendrite suppression . However, the safety characteristics are not just limited to solid-state vs lithium-ion thermal characteristics. Dendrite formation is also a critical part of the safety discussion. In Li-ion batteries, lithium ions from the electrolyte deposit unevenly on the surface of the anode, and once a nucleation site has been established, side reactions continue to add more lithium, leading to the formation of needle-like lithium chains called dendrites throughout the liquid electrolyte. The dendrites eventually grow enough that they pierce the separator membrane, connect the electrodes, and short circuit the cell causing thermal runaway. . While dendrite growth is still possible in solid-state batteries, their growth is significantly suppressed because of the mechanical properties of the cell. The rigid solid electrolyte has a high mechanical strength and therefore a high mechanical resistance to dendrite formation. The ceramic and sulphide compounds in the electrolyte are too hard for dendrites to penetrate, physically blocking dendrites from penetrating through the electrolyte and short-circuiting the cell. This leads to uniform lithium deposition on the electrode-electrolyte interface, and the only way that dendrites can penetrate through a solid-state electrolyte is if there are voids or grain boundaries for the dendrites to grow into and exploit. . Charging speed and lifespan compared. Charging speeds are continuing to improve for Li-ion batteries, especially with the likes of BYD now bringing flash charging to everyday EVs, enabling charging in under 10 minutes. This is currently the gold standard of Li-ion fast charging, and the average is much lower. As it stands, solid-state batteries are still firmly in development and have not been optimised to the level that Li-ion batteries have, so both semi-solid-state and solid-state battery charging speeds are currently below that of Li-ion batteries. . Future charging potential . However, with solid-state batteries containing both lithium metal anodes and high voltage cathodes, there is the potential for solid-state batteries to charge faster than Li-ion batteries in the future due to having a higher ionic conductivity—as this will help to facilitate faster energy charging rates. On the other hand, companies are currently marketing semi-solid-state batteries as 'solid-state', but while they have a higher energy density and safety, their charging rates might not be any better than Li-ion because of their mixed electrolyte structure which could limit ion migration. When ASSBs emerge commercially, it is likely to be a different story as they will just have a solid network to promote ionic conductivity. . As noted above, the average Li-ion EV fast charges from 10–80% SOC in 22–35 minutes, whereas it's anticipated that the average 10–80% SOC solid-state battery charging speed will be 10–15 minutes. . Cycle life advantages . When it comes to cycle life, solid-state battery cycle life is set to outperform Li-ion cycle life. While some cells like LFP have been designed for longevity and have a much higher cycle life, the average solid-state battery is going to last a lot longer than the average Li-ion battery with slower degradation rates. The average Li-ion battery lasts for 1,000–2,000 cycles before noticeable capacity loss, while solid-state battery cycle life could exceed 3,000–5,000 cycles before significant capacity loss occurs due to lower internal chemical reactivity and stress. For semi-solid-state batteries, the cycle life sits in between the two, with 1,500–2,500 cycles before noticeable capacity loss. . It should be noted that while these values for charging speeds and cycle life for ASSBs have been claimed by some manufacturers, because they are not yet at a stage of mass commercialisation, these claims cannot yet be independently verified at scale. . When will solid-state batteries actually be available?. As it stands in 2026, any 'solid-state' battery currently available today is semi-solid-state hybrid design and not a true ASSB. While it's great talking about the potential benefit of using solid-state batteries for EVs, one of the biggest questions is, when will solid-state batteries be available? The solid-state battery commercialisation timeline looks set to rapidly increase in the coming years, with the late 2020s (mostly around 2027–28) seeing many automakers and battery manufacturers undergoing small-scale production, while 2030 onwards will see these companies enter full-scale manufacturing. . A lot of progress has been made by automakers and battery manufacturers towards the commercialisation of solid-state batteries, and their commercial reality is now just around the corner. The progression will naturally start with lower volumes of vehicles, with luxury models in traditional automakers and luxury brands likely to be first to equip them due to the initial added cost before large-scale manufacturing is established. Once the scale is established, then the costs will come down and we will see mass production of the batteries and solid-state EVs. This will be at least by 2030, but could be as late as 2035 for some automakers, as different companies are working to different solid-state battery commercialisation timelines based on their current state of internal development. . Japanese automakers leading the charge. There's a lot of activity in Japan from the major legacy automakers. Toyota has stated that it aims to have its first solid-state batteries manufactured somewhere between 2027 and 2028, with them being included in its first vehicles by 2028. Toyota has claimed that its new solid-state battery will provide a 20% increase in range over the Toyota Performance battery and is expected to deliver 1,000 km of driving range and a 10–80% charging time of 10 minutes, with a second generation planned for further down the line with 1,200 km driving range. . . Honda has stated that it plans to integrate solid-state batteries within the second half of 2020s, whereas Nissan already has an operational pilot plant line, with plans to launch solid-state battery EVs with an 800Wh/L volumetric energy density by 2028. On the other hand, Hyundai Motor Group is working towards longer solid-state battery commercialisation timelines, with no plans to launch solid-state battery EVs before 2030. . Chinese manufacturers accelerating development. As expected, there is also a lot of activity over in China, where the majority of EV batteries are already manufactured and where new battery innovations tend to first be commercialised at scale. Geely, a Volvo subsidiary, has plans to have a solid-state battery pack completed by 2026 with a 400Wh/kg energy density. On the other hand, Dongfeng has already completed a 0.2GWh production line, with batteries ready for vehicle use from this year onwards. Dongfeng has set mass-production targets for 2027 with the expectation that its first battery pack will deliver 350Wh/kg energy density and 1,000 km range. Developments are already taking place to develop a new battery pack with a 500Wh/kg energy density. . GAC Motors, one of the leading companies developing commercial-level graphene-based EV batteries, has plans to integrate solid-state batteries into its EVs sometime this year, with mass production planned for 2027–2030. It's expected that the batteries will provide between 500–1,000+ km depending on the EV. Qingtao Energy is planning to deliver solid-state batteries at scale by 2027, with energy densities of at least 400Wh/kg. . BYD has been doing some serious innovation with its Blade Batteries, and the Blade Battery 2.0 has become one of the highest performance Li-ion systems today. Nevertheless, BYD are still innovating in the solid-state battery space and plans to have its first EVs integrated with solid-state batteries in 2027. There are plans to follow this up with a demonstration phase between 2027–2029 and mass production targets have been set for 2030. . Global automakers joining the race. There are also many other global automakers with solid-state batteries on their commercialisation radar in the next 5–10 years. Mercedes Benz has started testing solid-state batteries developed in partnership with Factorial Energy. It's expected that the batteries will provide a driving range of at least 620 miles, and both mass production and market introduction targets have been set for before 2030. . BMW has been testing solid-state cells in its BMW i7 range and has since formed a partnership with Samsung SDI to support commercialisation. As it stands, BMW is planning to have solid-state batteries mass-produced by 2030. Karma Automotive is planning to launch one of the first 'ultra-luxury super cars' with a solid-state battery by 2027. Karma Automotive has stated that the first vehicle to use its solid-state battery will be the Karma Kaveya super-coupe. This is a big transition and statement as Karma Automotive doesn't currently manufacture battery EVs but does offer PHEVs. . Independent battery manufacturers. Outside of automakers who have dedicated their R&D teams to developing new solid-state batteries, there are also many independent battery manufacturing companies that are set to supply automakers with solid-state batteries as well. . Back in China, the largest battery manufacturer in the world, CATL, currently has a conservative solid-state battery commercialisation timeline with small batch production by 2027 and mass production by 2030. . In South Korea, SK On opened a pilot plant back in 2025 and is planning for mass production and commercialisation of 800Wh/L solid-state batteries by 2029. Between 2026 and 2028, SK On is going to be focused on pilot-scale development and OEM integration ahead of large-scale manufacturing. As noted above, Samsung SDI are working with BMW but are also targeting 900Wh/L anode-free solid-state battery mass production by 2027 after success with the pilot line in Suwon. It's expected that the batteries will first be used in premium vehicles in 2027, and while there are claims of mass production, it's expected that the volumes in 2027 will still be small. Samsung SDI already supplies semi-solid-state batteries. . Finally, QuantumScape, who are backed by Volkswagen, is planning small-scale production in 2026 with mass production in 2027–2028. QuantumScape claims that its anode-free solid-state batteries have an 844Wh/L volumetric energy density, 301Wh/kg gravimetric energy and a 10–80% charge time of around 12 minutes. The company has claimed that EVs that achieve 350 miles on current Li-ion batteries could achieve up to 500 miles of range using its solid-state cells. . Frequently Asked Questions. Is solid-state safer than lithium-ion? . Yes. Solid-state batteries use a solid electrolyte instead of a flammable liquid one, which removes the main driver of thermal runaway and fire risk. They are also far more resistant to dendrite formation and can operate safely at higher internal temperatures (up to 80°C versus roughly 50°C for Li-ion), making them the next major step up in EV battery safety. . When will solid-state batteries actually be available? . Small-scale production is expected in the late 2020s, mostly around 2027-2028, from automakers including Toyota, Nissan, and BYD. True full-scale mass manufacturing of all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) isn’t expected until 2030 onwards, with some automakers not reaching mass production until 2035. Batteries marketed as “solid-state” today are typically semi-solid-state hybrids, not true ASSBs. . What solid-state batteries mean for EV charging infrastructure. So, with solid-state batteries on the horizon in the next 5–10 years, what does this mean for charging infrastructure? . There will need to be some EV infrastructure planning for solid-state batteries, but there won't necessarily need to be any dedicated solid-state battery charging infrastructure in the near-term. EVs with solid-state batteries will still be able to use the same charging standards (CCS, NACS, J1772), meaning that infrastructure compatibility is not going to be an issue. . Grid management considerations . While the charging speeds are not as high as Li-ion yet, in the future, they could become greater. At this point, charging station owners might have to think about their infrastructure as faster charging speeds could affect station throughput planning and dwell-time assumptions, as well as draw shorter but larger loads from the grid—which will need to be planned for and managed as this could lead to higher power spikes that could put pressure on the grid if a lot of these spikes happen all at once or for long time periods. For infrastructure owners, the safer batteries will mean that there is less fire risk, so multiple ultra-fast chargers on a site will eventually pose less of a fire risk as the ratio of EVs with solid-state batteries on the road increases. . Station design evolution . With different types of batteries on the road, charging stations will need to be able to accommodate EVs with differing voltages and power requirements so that power can be delivered safely and reliably. It will also mark a shift in consumer behaviour because there will be fewer stops for EV drivers. This could mean that charging stations might need to be redesigned to accommodate the shorter dwell times, because while drivers might stop less, the faster charging times could lead to a higher throughput of vehicles each day—so the layout should be maximised to make it easy for EVs to go in and out quickly. The increase in throughput could lead to higher returns for charging station owners and less downtime for fleets. . Energy storage integration . However, because of the potential for the high throughput to cause a lot of power spikes, either at once or continuously throughout the day, on-site renewables and BESS will have to become standard to act as a buffer to these spikes and prevent the destabilisation of the local grid. Some charging stations are already equipped with renewables and BESS but their integration as key energy assets is only going to increase as more solid-state battery EVs hit the road. . . . New battery technologies are proliferating as demand for safe and efficient energy storage solutions increases. Solid-state batteries (SSBs) represent a major advancement in energy storage technology with the potential to overcome several limitations of traditional lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). By replacing flammable liquid or gel electrolytes with solid materials such as ceramics, polymers, or sulfides, solid-state batteries offer enhanced safety, superior thermal stability, and significantly higher energy densities, reaching up to 500 Wh/kg compared to 250 Wh/kg in conventional systems. The presence of a solid electrolyte not only enables the use of lithium metal anodes and high-capacity cathodes but also mitigates risks of high flammability, dendrite formation, electrolytic decomposition at high voltages, and leaks that plague liquid electrolyte-based batteries. . With the ability to last over 1,000 cycles — compared to 500 cycles in typical LIBs — solid-state batteries also promise longer lifespans. Their smaller footprint and potential for more compact design than LIBs make them ideal for use in electric vehicles (EVs), wearable electronics, medical devices like pacemakers, and aerospace applications. . We examined the CAS Content Collection TM , the largest human-curated repository of scientific information, to better understand the research landscape of solid-state batteries, and we found a clear shift from early-stage research to widespread scientific and commercial interest (see Figure 1). ‍. . Figure 1: Publication trends in the field of solid-state batteries. Data for 2025 is through July. Source: CAS Content Collection. . . In the early 2000s, activity was minimal, indicating that solid-state batteries were limited to fundamental research. However, around 2017, academic papers and patents rose sharply, reflecting growing technological maturity, market demand, and recognition of this technology as a solution to key limitations of conventional lithium-ion batteries. . Now, the slightly higher number of patents suggests that the field is moving beyond academic research toward commercial readiness, with companies securing intellectual property. The sharp growth of patents in recent years reflects urgent demand driven by the increase in EVs, grid-level storage of renewable energy, and the need for safer, high-performance energy solutions. Current momentum indicates that solid-state batteries have reached a critical point of research and investment, often seen just before major breakthroughs and widespread adoption. . Researchers conducting similar searches across materials databases and scientific literature can use CAS SciFinder to access structure-based queries and property filtering capabilities that support rapid identification of candidate materials while tracking emerging innovations in battery technology.. Find out more . . Asia leads in global battery innovation . To evaluate commercialization efforts within the SSB sector, we identified the top 15 companies based on their patenting activity (Figure 2a). Japanese firms such as Toyota and Panasonic lead with extensive patent portfolios, reflecting Japan’s early strategic investment in SSB technology and its strong alignment with the automotive industry. The presence of other major Asian companies such as LG Chem, Samsung SDI, and CATL further reinforces Asia’s leadership in global battery innovation (see Figure 2a). . The trends of commercial patent activity across countries reveal shifting innovation dynamics in the SSB field (Figure 2b). While Japan has maintained steady leadership through consistent investment and long-term research, China’s rapid rise in recent years marks a significant shift. This surge is driven not only by established firms but also by a wave of new entrants actively filing patents . . In contrast, the relatively lower patent activity from the United States and Germany, despite their strong automotive and tech industries, suggests differing strategic priorities or alternative approaches to intellectual property protection in the SSB domain.. ‍. . Figure 2a: Leading commercial entities identified by their number of patent publications related to solid-state batteries. The inset pie chart shows the volume of commercial patents published by countries/regions. . . Figure 2b: Yearly trends for commercial patent publications for the leading countries/regions. . . Advantages of solid-state electrolytes . Solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) are the core component of solid-state batteries (SSBs), functioning as ion-conducting solids that replace traditional liquid electrolytes. They enable the transport of lithium ions or other metal ions between the battery’s electrodes while physically separating them, ensuring both ionic conductivity and electrical insulation. . A noteworthy characteristic of solid-state electrolytes is their capacity to facilitate ion transport through crystallographic sites, where mobile ions can behave like fluid phases within a solid matrix. This structural feature underpins their high ionic mobility, which is essential for efficient battery performance. Solid-state electrolytes also offer significant advantages over liquid systems, including nonflammability, non-volatility, superior mechanical strength, and resilience under extreme temperatures. These features not only enhance safety and stability but also support the use of lithium metal anodes, which can dramatically increase energy density and battery lifespan. . Solid-state electrolytes can be broadly categorized into five main types based on their chemical composition: oxides, sulfides, polymers, nitrides, and halides. Each type exhibits distinct structural and electrochemical characteristics that influence their performance. Both organic and inorganic solid-state electrolytes have been extensively studied in recent years, leading to significant improvements in ionic conductivity, stability, and compatibility with electrodes. . Our analysis of the CAS Content Collection with tools including CAS SciFinder® illustrates the top 20 solid-state electrolytes categorized by type (Figure 3a) and year (Figure 3b). Among these, inorganic electrolytes, mainly oxides and sulfides, are leading in the publication landscape due to their superior ionic conductivity, enhanced safety, long cycle life, and excellent thermal stability. . ‍. . Figure 3a: Top 20 solid-state electrolytes categorized by type within publication volume. Source: CAS Content Collection. See footnote for abbreviations. ‍. . Figure 3b: Top 10 solid state electrolytes categorized by year within publication volume. Source: CAS Content Collection. See footnote for abbreviations. . . Oxide-based solid-state electrolytes . Oxide-based solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) are widely studied for next-generation solid-state batteries due to their excellent chemical, thermal, and electrochemical stability. These electrolytes are air- and moisture-stable, making them easier to handle and process. They can also withstand high operating voltages and temperatures without decomposition. . As shown in Figure 3, leading types of oxide solid state electrolytes include lithium lanthanum zirconium oxide, garnet-type (LLZO) , lithium aluminum titanium phosphate, NASICON-type (LATP), and lithium lanthanum titanium oxide, perovskite-type (LLTO), all offering high ionic conductivity (typically 10⁻⁴ to >10⁻³ S/cm) and robust mechanical properties. LLZO provides a wide electrochemical stability window and good compatibility with lithium metal, while LATP is non-toxic, cost-effective, and suitable for hybrid systems. LLTO offers high conductivity and strong mechanical strength, though its performance depends on ceramic microstructure. . Despite their promise, oxide-based electrolytes have several limitations. Their brittle and rigid structure make it difficult to process and achieve intimate contact with electrodes, often leading to high interfacial resistance and poor ionic transfer. This brittleness also makes them vulnerable to cracking under mechanical stress or volume changes during cycling. Additionally, their room-temperature conductivity is generally lower than that of sulfide-based electrolytes. . LLZO technology can suffer from moisture sensitivity and lithium dendrite formation, while LATP and LLTO are unstable in direct contact with lithium metal due to Ti⁴⁺ reduction. These issues can lead to short circuits, although they can be mitigated through interface engineering and protective coatings. Overall, oxide electrolytes are valued for their outstanding stability, safety, and compatibility with high-voltage cathodes, making them strong candidates for durable and thermally stable solid-state lithium battery systems. . . Sulfide-based solid-state electrolytes . Sulfide-based electrolytes are among the most promising materials for next-generation solid-state batteries because of their exceptionally high ionic conductivity , which can reach up to 10⁻² S/cm, comparable to or even exceeding that of liquid electrolytes. Their structures, typically containing sulfur-based anions like PS₄³⁻, create a highly polarizable and flexible lattice that allows fast lithium-ion migration. . Another major advantage of sulfide electrolytes is their soft and deformable nature, which enables them to form excellent interfacial contact with cathodes and anodes under mild pressure: something difficult to achieve with brittle oxide electrolytes. They can also be processed at low temperatures, making large-scale fabrication feasible. . As seen in Figure 3a, among sulfide-based electrolytes, argyrodites, lithium-phosphorous-sulfur (Li-P-S) and lithium germanium phosphorus sulfide (LGPS) are leading candidates for solid-state batteries. Argyrodites (Li₆PS₅X, X = Cl, Br, I) and Li–P–S systems (e.g., Li₃PS₄, Li₇P₃S₁₁) offer conductivities ranging from 10⁻⁴ to >10⁻³ S/cm, while LGPS (e.g. Li₁₀GeP₂S₁₂), a thio-LISICON material, reaches up to 10⁻² S/cm, rivaling liquid electrolytes. . Despite these benefits, sulfide-based electrolytes also face critical challenges. They are highly sensitive to air and moisture, decomposing to release toxic hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) gas, which complicates handling and processing. Their electrochemical stability window is narrow, leading to undesirable reactions at high-voltage cathodes and lithium metal anodes, which form resistive interphases and degrade performance over time. Nonetheless, with continued improvements through doping, surface coatings, and composite engineering, sulfide-based solid-state electrolytes remain at the forefront of research for achieving high-performance, safe, and energy-dense solid-state lithium batteries. . . Polymer-based solid-state electrolytes . Polymer-based electrolytes are used in solid state batteries because they offer a unique combination of flexibility, processability, and safety that inorganic electrolytes often lack. Unlike brittle oxide electrolytes, polymer electrolytes are soft and deformable, allowing them to form intimate contact with electrodes. They also enable thin, lightweight, and flexible battery designs, which are ideal for wearable and portable electronics. . Among polymer-based solid-state electrolytes, polyacrylonitrile (PAN), hexafluoropropylene- polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF-HFP), and poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) are leading materials. However, their ionic conductivity is generally lower than that of inorganic electrolytes, especially at room temperature, and they may suffer from limited electrochemical stability at high voltage. Their excellent flexibility, interfacial compatibility, and scalability still make polymer-based electrolytes an attractive and practical choice for solid-state and flexible lithium battery applications. . . Nitride- and halide-based solid-state electrolytes . Nitride- and halide-based electrolytes are emerging classes of materials explored for high-performance all-solid-state LIBs due to their high ionic conductivity and favorable electrochemical stability. As seen in Figure 3b, lithium nitride (Li₃N) and LiXO (X= Cl, Br, I) are the only nitrides and halides, respectively, in the top 20 solid-state electrolytes based on publication trends. . Li₃N offers exceptionally fast lithium-ion transport, with conductivities up to 10⁻³ S/cm at room temperature, because of its open crystal structures that provide continuous pathways for Li⁺ migration. They are also thermally stable and compatible with lithium metal anodes. LiXO is generally combined with other solid electrolytes or polymers to improve interfacial contact and mechanical flexibility. . These materials also face notable drawbacks. Nitride- and halide-based solid-state electrolytes are highly reactive with moisture and air, producing toxic and corrosive byproducts like ammonia and HCl, which complicates handling and processing. Despite these limitations, nitride and halide electrolytes remain promising avenues for developing high-energy-density, and thermally robust solid-state lithium batteries, particularly when incorporated into composite electrolyte systems. . . Argyrodites emerge as the leading solid-state electrolyte technology . We further analyzed the publication trends for the top 10 solid-state electrolyte materials, and it revealed a fascinating shift in research focus in just the last few years (see Figure 3b). LLZO garnet-type electrolytes dominated the field until recently, attracting sustained attention from the research community due to their excellent stability against lithium metal and wide electrochemical window. However, a dramatic transformation occurred in 2021, with sulfide-based argyrodites experiencing an explosive surge in research interest that has propelled them past LLZO to become the most studied solid electrolyte system in 2024. . This remarkable ascent of argyrodites reflects several fundamental advantages that have become apparent to researchers. While LLZO requires extremely high sintering temperatures and struggles with interfacial contact issues due to its ceramic nature, argyrodites offer mechanical ductility that enables intimate contact with electrode materials through simple cold pressing. The sulfide framework provides ionic conductivities that significantly exceed those of oxide-based systems at room temperature, addressing one of the critical bottlenecks for solid-state battery commercialization. . Furthermore, the processing compatibility of argyrodites with existing battery manufacturing infrastructure has made them attractive for industrial-scale usage; they can be processed at moderate temperatures and even through solution-based methods. Meanwhile, other solid electrolyte systems like LATP and polymer-based electrolytes continue to attract steady but more modest research attention, suggesting that while these materials remain relevant, the field has identified argyrodites as offering the most promising near-term path toward practical solid-state batteries. . . Leading combinations of solid-state materials . Our analysis of the publication landscape also explored different types of solid-state batteries (SSBs) and the top solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) associated with them (see Figure 4). LIBs dominate the landscape with the highest volume of documents, representing approximately 80% of all research activity for solid-state batteries. The nearly equal split between journal publications and patent families indicates a mature field transitioning from fundamental research toward commercialization. ‍. . Figure 4: Distribution of solid-state battery research across different battery chemistries and associated solid-state electrolytes. Individual pie charts indicate the proportion of journal (J) and patent (P) publications for the respective batteries. Heat map tables show the most prevalent solid-state electrolytes associated with their respective solid-state batteries. Source: CAS Content Collection. See footnotes for abbreviations. . . The top solid-state electrolytes for lithium systems show interesting diversity. The oxide-based electrolytes LLZO and LATP receive the highest attention, followed by polymer electrolytes like PAN, sulfide-based argyrodites, and Li-P-S systems. This variety suggests the field hasn't converged on a single winning technology, with different solid-state electrolytes being explored for various application requirements. . Sodium-ion solid-state batteries come second in document volume, though they are still trailing lithium systems significantly. The patent-to-journal ratio favors journal publications slightly, indicating this field remains more research-focused than commercially driven. The electrolyte preferences for sodium systems show notable differences from lithium: NaZPSi (sodium super ionic conductor) leads the pack, while polymer electrolytes (PAN, PMMA) feature prominently. Some lithium-focused electrolytes like LATP and LLZO are also present, suggesting researchers are exploring cross-compatibility between systems. . Zinc-ion batteries represent the third significant player, showing a much higher proportion of journal publications compared to patents. This journal-heavy distribution suggests zinc solid-state batteries are still in the fundamental research phase, with researchers working to understand and optimize these systems before commercial development. The solid-state electrolyte landscape for zinc batteries is dominated by polymer electrolytes (PAN, PEO, PMMA), which makes sense given zinc's compatibility with aqueous and quasi-solid systems . . Emerging battery chemistries like magnesium and potassium show balanced research and patent activity despite lower overall numbers, indicating early stage but promising development. These systems could represent future alternatives as researchers seek to diversify beyond lithium, particularly for specific applications where their unique properties offer advantages. . The heat map intensities across different electrolytes, shown in Figure 4, reveal that while certain electrolytes show versatility across multiple battery types, others remain chemistry specific. This highlights the importance of tailored solid-state electrolyte development for each battery system's unique requirements. . . Patent trends show promising applications for solid-state batteries . Our analysis of publication volumes across application sectors for solid-state batteries (SSBs) reveals distinct patterns in research focus and commercialization maturity (see Figure 5). ‍. . Figure 5: Number of journal publications and patents for solid-state battery applications. Source: CAS Content Collection. . . Electronics and vehicles clearly dominate the field, representing approximately 75% of all application research. However, their development trajectories differ significantly. Electronics shows a notable gap between journal publications and patents, suggesting ongoing fundamental research challenges in adapting these batteries for consumer electronics. This could be related to miniaturization, cost, or manufacturing complexity. In contrast, the vehicle sector displays remarkable parity between publications and patents. Such findings indicate a mature field transitioning from laboratory to market, driven by the growth of EVs and the urgent need for safer, higher energy-density batteries. . Emerging application sectors show promise but remain predominantly research focused. Biomedical applications demonstrate substantial academic interest with limited patent activity, suggesting researchers are still exploring fundamental feasibility rather than pursuing commercialization. This could reflect the stringent regulatory requirements and biocompatibility challenges unique to medical devices. . Wearables show an even more pronounced research-to-patent gap, indicating that while the concept of flexible, safe solid-state batteries for wearable technology is academically intriguing, significant technical hurdles remain before commercial viability. . The aerospace sector features a nearly equal distribution of journal articles and patents. This balanced ratio, despite a lower overall volume of documents, mirrors the pattern observed in the vehicle sector. It suggests active commercial engagement driven by several compelling technical advantages of solid-state batteries in aerospace applications, such as nonflammability and better performance at high altitudes. . . Challenges and opportunities with solid-state batteries . Although solid-state batteries (SSBs) show great promise, several challenges prevent them from achieving large-scale commercialization. A major technical limitation is the relatively low ionic conductivity of many solid electrolytes at room temperature compared to liquid ones. Oxide-based electrolytes like LLZO require high sintering temperatures for dense microstructures, making processing complex and costly. Sulfide electrolytes offer high conductivity but are sensitive to air and moisture, necessitating inert conditions. . Another challenge is instability at the electrode–electrolyte interfaces. Unlike liquid electrolytes, solid–solid contact often results in poor interfacial contact and high resistance. Chemical reactions at these interfaces can form resistive layers, especially with lithium metal, worsening over cycles and degrading performance. The mechanical rigidity of solid electrolytes further contributes to stress, gaps, and delamination during volume changes, increasing impedance and performance decay. . Lithium dendrite formation remains a concern, as lithium filaments can propagate through microstructural defects in solid-state electrolytes under high current densities, causing short circuits. Additionally, large-scale production is costly — processing these materials requires high temperatures, high pressure, precise engineering, and dry conditions (especially for sulfides). These material and integration challenges, along recyclability issues and immature supply chains, hinder the transition from lab-scale prototypes to industrial-scale solid-state batteries. . Despite these hurdles, solid-state batteries are evolving toward a future where materials design, interface engineering, and scalable processing converge to deliver safer, denser, and longer-lasting energy storage. The next generation of these batteries will feature hybrid and composite electrolytes that combine the high conductivity of ceramics with the flexibility of polymers, ensuring stable interfaces and mechanical integrity during cycling. Advances in low-temperature fabrication, such as cold sintering and transient-liquid-assisted processing, will make manufacturing more efficient and compatible with large-scale production. . Recent prototypes reflect this momentum: Chery has unveiled a solid-state battery module with an energy density of 600 Wh/kg targeting 1,300 km range, more than double that of conventional lithium-ion batteries. Similarly, Sunwoda introduced a polymer all solid-state battery with 400 Wh/kg and a cycle life of 1,200 cycles under ultra-low pressure. This could give EVs ranges over 1,000 km and 1,200 cycles, enabling more than a decade of use, assuming annual driving of 20,000 km. . Meanwhile, data-driven approaches and AI-assisted materials discovery will accelerate optimization and quality control in this field. Beyond lithium, solid-state concepts extend to other metal ions such as sodium, zinc, magnesium, and potassium systems, broadening sustainability and resource accessibility. These continuous advancements and hybrid approaches are steadily closing the performance gap between traditional battery technology and new solid-state options. . Though full-scale deployment may still be years away, the convergence of scientific and industrial advances indicates that solid-state batteries are on track to reshape energy storage across industries in the coming decade. .
